issues.legal_issue: Compulsory acquisition for a trust scheme is an acquisition by the government when the government conducts the acquisition and the land vests in the trust only after the acquisition cost is paid.
material_facts: The land was acquired under the improvement legislation for a scheme promoted by the trust.
The legislation provided that the Collector would transfer the land to the trust upon payment of the acquisition cost, after which it would vest in the trust.
issues.conclusion: The government, rather than the trust, was the acquiring authority.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on section 59 of the Nagpur Improvement Trust Act, 1936, which provided for acquisition under the Land Acquisition Act as modified by that Act, and section 17-A inserted into the Land Acquisition Act by paragraph 6 of the Schedule. Section 17-A provided for the Collector to make over the land to the trust upon payment of the cost of acquisition; the Court treated this as showing that the acquisition was by the government, even though it was for the trust and could be initiated at its instance.

predicates.compulsory_acquisition_for_a_trust_schem: The land was compulsorily acquired for a scheme promoted by a trust.
predicates.government_pays_acquisition_cost_before_: The government conducted the acquisition, and the land vested in the trust only after the acquisition cost was paid.

issues.definition: When land is compulsorily acquired for a trust scheme and the government pays the acquisition cost before the land vests in the trust, the government is the acquiring authority.

issues.legal_issue: Compensation for compulsory acquisition cannot differ for equally situated owners merely because the land is acquired for a different public purpose, by a different authority, or under a different acquisition law.
material_facts: Land was acquired for a housing accommodation scheme under the improvement legislation, although the government could acquire land for the same purpose under the general acquisition law.

Under the improvement legislation, market value was limited to the use to which the land was being put, excluding potential value for another use, and the owner did not receive the additional amount ordinarily payable for compulsory acquisition.
The Court found that these disadvantages substantially outweighed the minor advantages under the improvement legislation.
issues.conclusion: The provisions producing the different compensation treatment violated Article 14; the appeal was dismissed, leaving the award set aside and the matter remitted for compensation to be determined according to law.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 permits reasonable legislative classification only when it rests on an intelligible differentia rationally related to a lawful legislative object. For compulsory acquisition, the purpose of acquisition, the identity of the acquiring authority, or the acquisition law ordinarily does not justify different compensation because those features do not warrant different treatment of the owner's individual right. The Court relied on Nandeshwar Prasad v. U.P. Govt., P. Vajravelu Mudaliar v. Special Deputy Collector, Madras, and Balammal v. State of Madras.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_compulsory_l: An owner challenged the legal validity of compensation treatment in a compulsory land acquisition proceeding.
predicates.land_could_be_acquired_under_either_regi: The government could acquire land for the relevant purpose under either of two available acquisition regimes.
predicates.equally_situated_owners_receive_differen: Owners in materially equivalent circumstances receive different compensation treatment.
predicates.compensation_difference_is_based_on_publ: The difference in compensation follows from the public purpose, acquiring authority, or acquisition law rather than a relevant difference in the owners' circumstances.

issues.definition: If an owner challenges compensation treatment in compulsory acquisition, the land could be acquired under either of two regimes, equally situated owners receive different compensation, and that difference rests on purpose, authority, or acquisition law, the differential compensation scheme is unconstitutional.

issues.legal_issue: The constitutional protection concerning laws implementing agrarian reform does not apply to the challenged acquisition for an urban housing scheme.
material_facts: The acquired land was taken for a housing accommodation scheme under the improvement legislation.
The acquisition was not for agrarian reform or for building a capital of a State.
issues.conclusion: Article 31A(1)(a) did not protect the challenged provisions from constitutional review.
issues.legal_principle: The Court stated that Article 31A(1)(a) is relevant to agrarian reforms and development and has no application to acquisition of land for building a capital of a State; it rejected reliance on that provision in this case.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_compulsory_l: An owner challenged the legal validity of provisions governing compulsory land acquisition.
predicates.acquisition_is_for_urban_housing_not_agr: The land was acquired for an urban housing scheme rather than for agrarian reform.

issues.definition: When a compulsory-acquisition challenge concerns land acquired for an urban housing scheme rather than agrarian reform, the agrarian-reform protection does not apply.
